newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: "Poor cousin" Philippines now Asia's hot pick.
newsitem.headline: "Poor cousin" Philippines now Asia's hot pick.

text.p: Strong growth has transformed the Philippines, once a poor cousin of booming Asian countries, into one of the hottest investment prospects in the region, currency dealers said on Thursday.

"If you trace back from 1994, the funds have been flowing in continuously, particularly this year," Jaime F. Panganiban, president of the Forex Philippines club, told Reuters at the two-day regional Asia-Pacific forex convention here.
"The confidence of investors has been established."
Speakers at the convention, which officially opened on Thursday, lauded the progress made by the Philippines. Giving the key note address was President Fidel Ramos.

"For four years now, GNP and GDP growth has been consistently rising," he said. "And now we believe we are on the threshold of sustained economic growth -- at levels to match the high growth rates of our East Asian neighbours," he added.
The Philippines recorded real growth of around 7.1 percent in the first half of this year, up from 5.5 percent in 1995.
Inflation has been declining steadily for the past eight months, hitting a low of 4.4 percent in September, against double-digit figures a year earlier.
"Right now, it's a country with very high yields on investments, one of the highest around, and this is what our clients want," said a Singapore bank dealer.

Interest on the 91-day Treasury bill, the benchmark interest rate, is currently 11.766 percent, while the overnight rate is an average 14.56 percent. In contrast, Japan's official discount rate is currently at 0.5 percent.
As a result, even risk-shy Japanese investors were turning bullish on the Philippines, Tokyo fund managers said.

"The Philippine market is extremely attractive right now... It is a still a small market, but it is a very good chance for those of us who want to invest," said Kimiharu Fujisawa, a manager at Yamaichi Investment Trust Management.

Fujisawa said he felt the Philippines was now the third best investment opportunity in Asia after Hong Kong and Malaysia, with "quite a lot of interest" in the housing and utilities sectors, and more limited although still good potential in construction.

But actual investment in the Philippines remains limited. Figures issued by the Investment Trusts Association of Japan show that outstanding holdings of Philippine stocks by investment trust fund management firms stood at 23 billion yen ($206 million) at the end of September out of total Asian stock holdings of 591.3 billion yen.
And not all fund managers are optimistic about the country.
"A lot of the recent economic gains have been made on export growth, and there's some doubt about how sustainable that is," one fund manager said.
